About

Current version: solar system simulation v_1.0 (28 October 2026)

This simulation is for scientific and educational purposes. It is also a support software for the book "Marea greșeală a „marelui” Einstein" by Ovidiu Bidian (Artpress, ISBN 978-973-108-587-6).

What is real in this simulation:

  • the motion of the Sun through absolute space, as science sees it today (2026): the Sun moves around the center of our galaxy, the Milky Way, on a huge orbit with a radius of about 26 000 light years, at about 230 km/s, one turn in about 230 million years. It moves towards the constellation Cygnus, at about 60° to the plane of the planets' orbits (the ecliptic), so the trails leave that plane at this angle. The absolute space of this simulation is a cylinder around the Sun's path. In this simulation the time frame of absolute space is about 165 years (one revolution of Neptune: the trails need that long to reach the wall of the space), so the path of the Sun through absolute space is a straight line. The trajectories of the celestial bodies through absolute space are represented by their yellow trails;
  • the orbits of the celestial bodies (Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Pluto) around the Sun: real orbital elements (JPL, epoch J2000), real periods, real sizes of the celestial bodies;
  • the motion of the planets on their orbits obeys Kepler's laws;
  • the rotation axes of the celestial bodies: real directions in space (for example Pluto's axis is tilted about 120° from the axis of its orbit, so Pluto spins backwards); the views around a celestial body use its real equator and rotation poles;
  • the surfaces of the celestial bodies: real maps (Pluto: NASA / JHUAPL / SwRI, New Horizons; Earth, Mars, Jupiter: Solar System Scope);
  • the light: the celestial bodies are lit by the Sun, from the center of the Sun.

What is not real in this simulation:

  • the background stars: placed at random, with random brightness (the real constellations will come later);
  • the spin of the celestial bodies: every celestial body turns once every 10 seconds, at every simulation speed (Pluto really turns once in about 6.4 Earth days);
  • the apparent size of the celestial bodies: a minimum apparent radius is set, so that a celestial body can be seen also from far away;
  • the dark side of the celestial bodies: lit a little, as the Earth's night side by a full Moon, so that its surface can be seen;
  • the celestial bodies move on independent orbits (they do not attract each other), and only a few of them are shown.

This software was made by Claude Code under the direct and close requirements and supervision of a human, Ovidiu Bidian.
And no, AI will not kill us all by 2030 — human stupidity might.
One (important) note: the term "artificial intelligence" is not correct; it should be replaced with "artificial thinking", because this is what AI actually does.
